lessons.title: Water Requirements at Different Growth Stages
lessons.body:
Sunflower needs different amounts of water as it grows. From planting to emergence, the seed needs enough moisture to sprout, but too much water can rot it. In most African conditions, you need about 20-30 mm of water in the first 10 days after planting. If you plant with the first rains, you may not need to irrigate. But if you plant in dry conditions, a light irrigation of 15-20 mm is enough to get the seed going.

From emergence to the vegetative stage (about 20 to 40 days after planting), the plant grows leaves and roots. Water use increases. The crop needs about 3-4 mm of water per day. In total, this stage may need 80-120 mm of water. If rainfall is low, you should irrigate every 5-7 days, applying 25-30 mm each time. The roots are still shallow, so don't let the top 30 cm of soil dry out completely.

The flowering stage (40 to 70 days after planting) is the most critical. Sunflower uses 5-7 mm of water per day. A shortage now means fewer seeds and smaller heads. Total water needed during flowering is about 150-200 mm. You must keep the soil moist. In dry spells, irrigate every 4-5 days with 30-35 mm. Do not let the plant wilt at midday, as this reduces seed set.

During seed fill (70 to 100 days), water use drops slightly to 4-5 mm per day, but it is still important. Lack of water now causes empty seeds and low oil content. The crop needs about 100-150 mm during this stage. Irrigate every 6-7 days with 25-30 mm if rains fail. As the plant matures and heads turn brown, reduce watering. Too much water late can delay maturity and cause head rot.

In total, a sunflower crop needs 500-700 mm of water from planting to harvest. In dry African regions like the Sahel or northern Kenya, you must irrigate to reach this. In wetter areas, rainfall may supply most of it. Always check your soil: sandy soils need more frequent, smaller amounts; clay soils hold water longer but can become waterlogged. A simple rain gauge or a marked stick in a container can help you track rainfall and irrigation.

lessons.title: Irrigation Scheduling Based on Soil Moisture and ET
lessons.body:
Irrigation scheduling means deciding when to water and how much. You can do this by checking soil moisture or by using evapotranspiration (ET) data. ET is the water lost from soil and plants to the air. In hot, dry African conditions, ET can be 5-8 mm per day. If you know ET, you know how much water your crop has used and needs to be replaced.

A simple way to check soil moisture is the feel method. Take a handful of soil from 15 cm deep. If it forms a ball and leaves a slight moisture mark on your hand, it has enough water. If it crumbles and feels dry, you need to irrigate. For sandy soil, squeeze a sample: if it holds together, it's moist enough; if it falls apart, irrigate. For clay, roll it into a ribbon: if it makes a ribbon, it's too wet; if it breaks, it's dry. Do this test every 2-3 days in the root zone.

You can also use a simple tensiometer, a tool that measures how tightly soil holds water. Install it at 20 cm depth. When the reading is between 30 and 50 centibars (cb), it's time to irrigate. Tensiometers cost about $50-100 and are available in agricultural supply shops in many African cities. If you can't afford one, a homemade gypsum block or even a wooden dowel painted with water-sensitive paint can work.

ET-based scheduling uses local weather data. Many African meteorological departments provide daily ET estimates. If ET is 6 mm today, your crop used 6 mm of water. If your soil holds 100 mm of available water, you can wait until 50% is used (50 mm) before irrigating. That means you can go about 8 days (50 divided by 6) before irrigating. But during flowering, don't let depletion exceed 40%. So irrigate after 4-5 days.

Combine both methods: check soil moisture to confirm ET estimates. Keep a simple record: date, ET, rainfall, irrigation amount. After a season, you'll know your fields better. In Africa, where rainfall is unpredictable, scheduling saves water and money. It also prevents overwatering, which leaches nutrients and wastes fuel for pumps.

lessons.title: Irrigation Methods: Furrow, Sprinkler, and Drip
lessons.body:
Furrow irrigation is the oldest and cheapest method. You make small channels (furrows) between crop rows and let water flow. It works well on flat land with clay or loam soil. For sunflower, space furrows 75-90 cm apart, and let water run for 2-4 hours. But it uses a lot of waterâonly about 50-60% is used by the crop; the rest evaporates or seeps away. It also needs level land and a lot of labour to manage. In Africa, it's common in Egypt, Sudan, and along river valleys. To improve, use shorter furrows (30-50 m) and surge irrigation (alternate wetting and drying) to save water.

Sprinkler irrigation sprays water like rain. You can use hand-moved sprinklers, which are affordable and good for small farms. A typical sprinkler covers a 12-15 m circle. You move it every 30-60 minutes. It uses 70-80% of water efficiently. But in hot, windy areas, up to 30% can evaporate before hitting the ground. So irrigate early morning or evening. Sprinklers are good for sandy soils and uneven land. They also help cool the crop during heat stress. However, they can spread diseases if leaves stay wet. In Kenya, smallholder sunflower farmers often use bucket sprinklers or micro-sprinklers.

Drip irrigation is the most efficientâ90-95% of water reaches the roots. Water drips slowly from emitters along a pipe placed near the plant. It saves water, reduces weeds, and works on any soil. But the initial cost is high: about $500-1000 per acre for the kit. In Africa, governments and NGOs sometimes subsidize drip kits. A simple gravity-fed drip system using a raised tank (1-2 m high) can cost less. For sunflower, place one drip line per row, with emitters every 30 cm. Run it for 1-2 hours every 2-3 days. Drip is excellent for dry regions and for farmers who want to grow sunflower in the off-season.

Choose based on your water supply, soil, and budget. If water is scarce, drip is best. If labour is cheap and water is plentiful, furrow works. Many African farmers combine methods: furrow for the main field and drip for a small vegetable plot. Always maintain your systemâclean sprinkler nozzles and drip filters, and repair leaks. A well-managed system saves water and gives better yields.

lessons.title: Critical Irrigation Periods: Flowering and Seed Fill
lessons.body:
Sunflower is most sensitive to water stress during flowering and seed fill. These two stages, from about 40 to 100 days after planting, determine your yield. If the plant lacks water now, you lose seeds, oil content, and head size. Even a short dry spell of 3-4 days during flowering can cut yields by 20-30%. So you must plan your irrigation to ensure water is available at these critical times.

Flowering starts when the first petals open and lasts about 2-3 weeks. During this time, the plant needs 5-7 mm of water per day. The soil should be kept moist to a depth of 60 cm. If you use furrow irrigation, apply 30-35 mm every 4-5 days. With sprinklers, run them for 2-3 hours every 3-4 days. With drip, run for 2-3 hours daily or every other day. Never let the plant wilt at middayâif you see wilting, irrigate immediately. Also, avoid overhead irrigation during full bloom, as it can wash away pollen and reduce pollination. Use drip or furrow instead.

Seed fill begins after flowering and lasts about 30-40 days. The seeds are filling with oil, and water stress now causes empty, shriveled seeds. The crop needs 4-5 mm per day. Keep the soil moist but not waterlogged. Irrigate every 5-6 days with 25-30 mm. If you stop watering too early, seeds won't fill properly. But if you water too late, when heads are turning brown, you risk head rot and delayed harvest. So reduce irrigation as the backs of heads turn yellow.

In African conditions, these critical periods often coincide with dry spells. In the Sahel, the rainy season may end before seed fill, so you need stored water or a well. In East Africa, the short rains may fail during flowering. Always have a backup plan: a small pond, a borehole, or a water tank. A simple soil moisture test (feel method) during these stages is essential. If the soil is dry at 15 cm, irrigate. Don't wait for the plant to show stressâby then, yield is already lost.

Remember: water during flowering and seed fill is not just about survival; it's about profit. Every millimeter of water applied correctly at these stages gives you more seeds and higher oil. So prioritize these periods in your irrigation schedule, even if it means using more water then and less at other times.

lessons.title: Drainage and Waterlogging Prevention
lessons.body:
Sunflower hates waterlogged soil. It can survive short floods, but if water stands for more than 2-3 days, roots suffocate, and the plant turns yellow, wilts, and dies. Waterlogging also causes root rot and fungal diseases. In Africa, heavy rains or over-irrigation can waterlog fields, especially on flat, clay soils. So you must ensure good drainage.

First, choose well-drained land. Avoid low spots where water collects. If your field is flat, make raised beds or ridges. For sunflower, plant on ridges 20-30 cm high. This keeps the root zone above standing water. In furrow irrigation, make sure furrows drain at the endâdig a shallow ditch to carry excess water away. On sloping land, use contour ridges to slow water and prevent erosion, but also allow drainage.

If your soil is clay and drains poorly, add organic matter like compost or manure. This improves soil structure and lets water move through. You can also install subsurface drainage: dig trenches 60-80 cm deep, fill with gravel, and lay a perforated pipe, then cover with soil. This is expensive but lasts for years. A cheaper method is to plant on broad beds and keep furrows open. In the rainy season, check your field after every heavy rain. If water stands for more than a few hours, open a channel to drain it.

Over-irrigation is a common cause of waterlogging. Never apply more water than the soil can hold. For sandy soil, apply 20-25 mm per irrigation; for clay, 30-35 mm. If you see puddles or runoff, stop. Use a simple rain gauge to measure irrigation. Also, avoid irrigating just before expected heavy rain. Check the weather forecastâmany African meteorological services send free SMS alerts.

Signs of waterlogging: yellowing leaves, stunted growth, wilting even when soil is wet, and rotten roots. If you see these, stop watering and improve drainage immediately. You can also plant sunflower on ridges and use furrow irrigation with a drain at the end. In extreme cases, you may need to replant. Prevention is better: prepare your land with drainage in mind before planting. A well-drained field gives higher yields and healthier plants.

lessons.title: Water Use Efficiency and Conservation Practices
lessons.body:
Water is scarce in many parts of Africa. To grow sunflower profitably, you must use every drop wisely. Water use efficiency (WUE) means getting more seed per unit of water. You can improve WUE by reducing evaporation, using better irrigation methods, and conserving soil moisture. A sunflower crop with good WUE can produce 1.5-2 kg of seed per cubic meter of water. With poor management, it may be only 0.5 kg.

Mulching is one of the cheapest ways to save water. Spread crop residues, dry grass, or plastic mulch between rows. A 5-10 cm layer of organic mulch can reduce evaporation by 30-50%. It also cools the soil and suppresses weeds. In dry areas like northern Nigeria or Senegal, mulching is a game-changer. You can also use living mulch like cowpea, but avoid competition for water.

Improve your irrigation method. Drip irrigation saves 30-50% water compared to furrow. If you use furrow, surge irrigation (alternating wet and dry cycles) can save 20-30%. Sprinklers at night or early morning reduce evaporation losses. Also, fix leaks promptly. A single dripping emitter can waste 20-30 liters per day. Maintain your pump and pipes.

Conserve soil moisture by reducing tillage. No-till or minimum tillage leaves crop residues on the surface, which shade the soil and slow evaporation. It also improves water infiltration. In Ethiopia and Kenya, farmers using conservation agriculture with sunflower have seen better yields in dry years. Plant windbreaksâtrees like Grevillea or Acaciaâto reduce wind speed and evaporation. But don't shade the sunflower too much.

Harvest rainwater. Dig small ponds, trenches, or half-moons (zai pits) to capture runoff. In the Sahel, zai pits filled with manure and planted with sunflower have doubled yields in dry spells. You can also use roof catchment to fill a tank for supplemental irrigation. A 5,000-liter tank can irrigate 0.1 hectare for a few critical days.

Finally, schedule irrigation based on need, not habit. Use the feel method or ET data. Water early morning or evening. Keep records of water used and yield. After a season, calculate your WUE: total seed (kg) divided by total water (mÂ³). Try to improve it each year. Efficient water use not only saves money but also makes your farm more resilient to drought.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Water Management and Irrigation for Sunflower Farming in Africa

Water is the single most controllable input in sunflower production, and in most of Africa it is also the most expensive and scarce. A sunflower crop that receives the right amount of water at the right time can yield 2.5â3.5 t/ha under good management, while the same crop under drought stress during flowering may yield less than 0.8 t/ha. For the commercial grower, the difference between profit and loss often comes down to irrigation scheduling, method selection and drainage â not seed or fertiliser. This practical reference consolidates the key decisions from the six lessons in this module into a single field-ready guide.

1. Water Requirements at Different Growth Stages

Sunflower is often described as drought-tolerant, but this is misleading for commercial production. The crop has a deep taproot (up to 2 m) that allows it to access subsoil moisture, yet its yield is highly sensitive to water stress at two specific windows. Total seasonal water requirement ranges from 450â650 mm depending on climate, with peak daily use of 6â8 mm/day during flowering.

Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen et al., 1998), Table 12; validated with sunflower trials cited in FAO Land & Water Bulletin 33.

2. Irrigation Scheduling Based on Soil Moisture and ET

Two practical methods dominate African commercial sunflower production. The first is soil moisture monitoring â using a tensiometer, gypsum block or simple hand-feel test at 30 cm and 60 cm depth. Irrigate when soil moisture drops below 50% of field capacity in the root zone. The second is ET-based scheduling: track reference evapotranspiration (ETo) from a local weather station or the FAO Penman-Monteith estimate, multiply by the Kc for the current stage, and replace that amount of water. In practice, most growers combine both: ET tells you how much, soil moisture tells you when.

Soil type Field capacity (mm/m) Irrigation trigger (tensiometer, kPa) Typical interval (flowering)
Sandy80â110â30 to â40Every 3â4 days
Sandy loam120â150â40 to â50Every 5â7 days
Loam / clay loam160â200â50 to â60Every 7â10 days
Clay180â220â60 to â70Every 10â14 days

Source: Based on FAO Irrigation Manual Module 4 (Savva & Frenken, 2002) and South African ARC-Grain Crops Institute sunflower irrigation guidelines.

3. Irrigation Methods: Furrow, Sprinkler, Drip

Method choice is a capital decision. Furrow is cheapest to install but has 40â60% efficiency and needs level land and labour. Sprinkler (including centre pivot and lateral move) achieves 70â85% efficiency and is the most common method on large commercial sunflower farms in South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Drip achieves 90â95% efficiency and is best for high-value rotations or water-scarce areas, but the capital cost (US$1,500â3,000/ha) rarely justifies it for sunflower alone â it is usually installed for a rotation including vegetables or seed crops.

Business note: Sunflower is a relatively low-value crop (US$300â500/t farmgate). Drip irrigation is only viable if sunflower is part of a rotation with higher-value crops, or if water savings are monetised through water trading or reduced pumping costs.

4. Critical Irrigation Periods: Flowering and Seed Fill

The two non-negotiable windows are flowering (R5âR6) and seed fill (R7âR8). Water stress during flowering causes flower abortion, poor pollination and reduced head size â yield losses of 30â50% are common. Stress during seed fill reduces oil content and 1,000-seed weight. If water is limited, prioritise these stages over vegetative growth. A single well-timed irrigation at flowering can add 0.5â1.0 t/ha compared to no irrigation.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Water & Chemical Handling

Never irrigate immediately after applying herbicides or pesticides if the label prohibits it â runoff can contaminate drinking water sources and cause crop damage. When using drip or sprinkler systems with fertigation, wear gloves and eye protection; concentrated fertiliser solutions can cause chemical burns. In areas with schistosomiasis (bilharzia) or malaria, avoid prolonged contact with canal and furrow water, and treat standing water sources. Ensure pumps and electrical connections are earthed and inspected annually â electrocution in flooded fields is a leading cause of farm fatalities in irrigated African agriculture.

5. Drainage and Waterlogging Prevention

Sunflower is more sensitive to waterlogging than to drought. Just 48â72 hours of standing water during vegetative growth can reduce yield by 20â40%, and waterlogging during flowering can be catastrophic. In high-rainfall areas (e.g. parts of Tanzania, Uganda, Malawi), land preparation must include drainage furrows at 10â20 m spacing, and raised beds for heavy clay soils. In irrigated schemes, avoid over-irrigation â apply only the calculated ETc replacement and monitor for ponding after each event.

6. Water Use Efficiency and Conservation Practices

Water use efficiency (WUE) is measured as kg grain per mm of water. Good commercial sunflower achieves 4â7 kg/mm/ha; poor management achieves 1â2 kg/mm/ha. Key practices: (1) mulch or conserve crop residue to reduce evaporation; (2) irrigate early morning or evening to cut evaporation losses by 20â30%; (3) use deficit irrigation strategically â reduce water during vegetative stage, never during flowering; (4) maintain soil organic matter to improve water-holding capacity; (5) repair leaks in canals and pipes â 15â25% of water is lost in poorly maintained furrow systems; (6) use soil moisture sensors rather than calendar scheduling.

  • â Install at least one tensiometer or moisture sensor per 5 ha block.
  • â Calculate daily ETc = ETo Ã Kc for the current growth stage.
  • â Never let sunflower suffer stress during flowering (R5âR6) or seed fill (R7âR8).
  • â Irrigate early morning or late afternoon to reduce evaporation.
  • â Inspect and repair canals, pipes and emitters weekly â leaks waste 15â25%.
  • â Ensure drainage furrows are open before the rainy season.
  • â Record every irrigation event: date, volume, duration, and crop stage.

quiz.q: How much water does sunflower need from planting to emergence?
quiz.explanation: Sunflower needs about 20-30 mm of water in the first 10 days after planting for good germination.

quiz.q: During which growth stage does sunflower use the most water per day?
quiz.explanation: Flowering stage uses 5-7 mm per day, the highest daily water use.

quiz.q: What is the total water requirement for a sunflower crop from planting to harvest?
quiz.explanation: Sunflower needs 500-700 mm of water in total for a full season.

quiz.q: Which soil type needs more frequent but smaller irrigations?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils hold less water, so they require more frequent, smaller applications.

quiz.q: What does ET stand for in irrigation scheduling?
quiz.explanation: ET is evapotranspiration, the water lost from soil and plants to the air.

quiz.q: In the feel method, what does it mean if a handful of soil forms a ball and leaves a moisture mark?
quiz.explanation: A ball that holds together with a moisture mark indicates adequate moisture for irrigation.

quiz.q: What is the ideal tensiometer reading range to irrigate sunflower?
quiz.explanation: A tensiometer reading of 30-50 centibars indicates it's time to irrigate.

quiz.q: If ET is 6 mm per day and your soil holds 100 mm available water, how many days can you wait before irrigating at 50% depletion?
quiz.explanation: 50% of 100 mm is 50 mm; 50 divided by 6 mm/day equals about 8 days.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method is the oldest and cheapest?
quiz.explanation: Furrow irrigation is the oldest and least expensive method.

quiz.q: What is the water use efficiency of furrow irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Furrow irrigation is only about 50-60% efficient due to evaporation and seepage.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method delivers water most efficiently to the roots?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation is 90-95% efficient, delivering water directly to the root zone.

quiz.q: What is a major disadvantage of sprinkler irrigation in hot, windy areas?
quiz.explanation: Up to 30% of water can evaporate before reaching the ground in hot, windy conditions.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a drip irrigation kit per acre?
quiz.explanation: A drip irrigation kit costs about $500-1000 per acre, though subsidies may reduce this.

quiz.q: During which stage is sunflower most sensitive to water stress?
quiz.explanation: Flowering and seed fill are the critical periods when water stress most reduces yield.

quiz.q: How much can yield be reduced by a 3-4 day dry spell during flowering?
quiz.explanation: A short dry spell during flowering can cut yields by 20-30%.

quiz.q: Why should overhead irrigation be avoided during full bloom?
options: D) It cools the plant too much
quiz.explanation: Overhead irrigation during full bloom can wash away pollen and reduce pollination.

quiz.q: What happens if sunflower is water-stressed during seed fill?
quiz.explanation: Water stress during seed fill causes empty, shriveled seeds and lower oil content.

quiz.q: When should you reduce irrigation for sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Reduce irrigation as heads turn brown to prevent head rot and delay maturity.

quiz.q: How long can sunflower survive in waterlogged soil before dying?
quiz.explanation: Sunflower can survive short floods but dies if water stands for more than 2-3 days.

quiz.q: What is a cheap method to prevent waterlogging on flat land?
quiz.explanation: Planting on ridges 20-30 cm high keeps the root zone above standing water.

quiz.q: What is a sign of waterlogging in sunflower?
options: A) Wilting when soil is wet
quiz.explanation: Wilting even when soil is wet is a classic sign of waterlogged roots.

quiz.q: How much can organic mulch reduce evaporation?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer of organic mulch can reduce evaporation by 30-50%.

quiz.q: What is surge irrigation?
options: B) Alternating wet and dry cycles
quiz.explanation: Surge irrigation alternates wetting and drying cycles in furrows to save water.

quiz.q: What is a zai pit?
options: B) A planting hole for water harvesting
quiz.explanation: Zai pits are planting holes that capture runoff and concentrate water and nutrients.

quiz.q: What is the formula for water use efficiency (WUE)?
options: C) Water used x seed yield
quiz.explanation: WUE is calculated as seed yield (kg) divided by water used (mÂ³).

quiz.q: Which practice conserves soil moisture by leaving crop residues on the surface?
quiz.explanation: No-till or minimum tillage leaves residues that shade soil and reduce evaporation.

quiz.q: How much water can a 5,000-liter tank provide for supplemental irrigation?
quiz.explanation: A 5,000-liter tank can irrigate about 0.1 hectare for a few critical days.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of planting windbreaks around sunflower?
options: B) Reduces wind speed and evaporation
quiz.explanation: Windbreaks reduce wind speed, which lowers evaporation and protects plants.

quiz.q: When is the best time to irrigate to reduce evaporation?
quiz.explanation: Irrigating early morning or evening minimizes water loss to evaporation.

quiz.q: What is the first step to improve water use efficiency on your farm?
options: B) Schedule irrigation based on need
quiz.explanation: Scheduling irrigation based on crop need, not habit, is fundamental to water use efficiency.
